title: 2 Chronicles 36:1–10
context: After Josiah, Joahaz reigns three months before the king of Egypt removes him, fines the land, and makes his brother Eliakim king as Jehoiakim. Nebuchadnezzar binds Jehoiakim to take him to Babylon and carries off temple vessels, and Jehoiachin reigns three months and ten days before he too is taken to Babylon and Zedekiah is made king. Both traditions read this as shared ground on Judah’s swift decline; 2 Kings 23:31–24:17 is the parallel, and Jehoiakim’s end, Jehoiachin’s age, and Zedekiah’s relationship differ from it in ways noted without resolution.

verses.text: Then the people of the land took Jehoahaz the son of Josiah, and made him king in his father’s place in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then the people of the land took Jehoahaz the son of Josiah, and made him king in his father’s place in Jerusalem.” Arminian readers note that the people act to secure the succession (cf. 2 Kings 23:30).

Their choice is quickly undone.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the beginning of rapid instability after Josiah’s death.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, consistent with the notes on 2 Kings 23:30: the people’s choice begins the final chapter of Judah’s kings.

verses.text: Joahaz was twenty-three years old when he began to reign; and he reigned three months in Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Joahaz was twenty-three years old when he began to reign; and he reigned three months in Jerusalem.” Arminian readers note the brevity of the reign.

The figures match 2 Kings 23:31.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a short reign under foreign pressure.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the Chronicler gives no evaluation of Joahaz, while 2 Kings 23:32 says he did evil.

verses.text: The king of Egypt removed him from office at Jerusalem, and fined the land one hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The king of Egypt removed him from office at Jerusalem, and fined the land one hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold.” Arminian readers note Judah’s loss of independence.

The tribute matches 2 Kings 23:33.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see Judah now subject to Egypt.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the burden of tribute falls on the land, as the notes on 2 Kings 23:33–35 also observe.

verses.text: The king of Egypt made Eliakim his brother king over Judah and Jerusalem, and changed his name to Jehoiakim. Neco took Joahaz his brother, and carried him to Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The king of Egypt made Eliakim his brother king over Judah and Jerusalem, and changed his name to Jehoiakim.” Arminian readers note that a foreign king now chooses and renames Judah’s ruler.

Neco takes Joahaz to Egypt.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the loss of the kingdom’s independence.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: Jeremiah 22:10–12 is often understood as referring to the exiled Joahaz under the name Shallum, as noted at 2 Kings 23:31.

verses.text: Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. He did that which was evil in the LORD his God’s sight.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. He did that which was evil in the LORD his God’s sight.” Arminian readers note that he is held responsible for his own reign.

The figures match 2 Kings 23:36.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the verdict that marks the last kings.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: Josiah’s reform did not carry over to his sons.

verses.text: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against him, and bound him in fetters to carry him to Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against him, and bound him in fetters to carry him to Babylon.” Arminian readers note that Kings does not record this detail.

How this notice relates to 2 Kings 24:1–6 is discussed and left unresolved here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the difference and do not harmonize it.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, consistent with the notes on 2 Kings 24:6: Jehoiakim’s end is presented differently in the sources.

verses.text: Nebuchadnezzar also carried some of the vessels of the LORD’s house to Babylon, and put them in his temple at Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Nebuchadnezzar also carried some of the vessels of the LORD’s house to Babylon, and put them in his temple at Babylon.” Arminian readers note the beginning of the temple’s plunder (cf. Dan 1:1–2).

The vessels will later return (Ezra 1:7–11).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the vessels of God’s house placed in a foreign temple as a sign of judgment.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the loss is real but not final, as the return of the vessels shows.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Jehoiakim, and his abominations which he did, and that which was found in him, behold, they are written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah; and Jehoiachin his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
The rest of Jehoiakim’s acts, “and his abominations which he did, and that which was found in him,” are written in the book of the kings. Arminian readers note that the summary is negative.

The phrase “that which was found in him” is not explained.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a reign summarized by its abominations.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: “Jehoiachin his son reigned in his place,” continuing the decline.

verses.text: Jehoiachin was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned three months and ten days in Jerusalem. He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Jehoiachin was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned three months and ten days in Jerusalem.” Arminian readers note that 2 Kings 24:8 gives his age as eighteen.

The difference is noted without resolution.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the difference, as the notes on 2 Kings 24:8 do.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: “He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight,” and his reign is brief.

verses.text: At the return of the year, King Nebuchadnezzar sent and brought him to Babylon, with the valuable vessels of the LORD’s house, and made Zedekiah his brother king over Judah and Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
“At the return of the year, King Nebuchadnezzar sent and brought him to Babylon... and made Zedekiah his brother king.” Arminian readers note that 2 Kings 24:17 calls Zedekiah Jehoiachin’s father’s brother.

The difference in relationship is noted without resolution.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the Davidic king carried away with “the valuable vessels of the LORD’s house.”

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, consistent with the notes on 2 Kings 24:15–17: Judah’s throne is now in Babylon’s hands.
